lesson.title: Coupled change: two tanks and two masses

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the real dot staying the sum of two faint dots when you drag the start dot and press Go. Each faint dot rides its own eigenvector line at its own rate.
interactive.title: The state plane
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: On the left is the real thing. On the right is the state plane. It is a square of axes with one dot, whose two numbers are x₁ and x₂. A System choice picks one of three. When it picks a system the screen's words do not describe, a line says which system they describe. Open tanks are two 100 L tanks of brine. Fresh water runs into tank 1 at 15 L/min. A pump sends 20 L/min from tank 1 to tank 2. Another 5 L/min runs back. The other 15 L/min drains out of tank 2, so each tank stays at 100 L. Arrows show the flows. Each tank's salt is drawn as a shaded level, labelled x₁ or x₂. x₁ and x₂ are the grams of salt in tanks 1 and 2. Each flow carries salt at its tank's strength. That strength is the tank's grams divided by 100 L. What leaves a tank is minus and what arrives is plus. So x₁′ = −0.2x₁ + 0.05x₂ and x₂′ = 0.2x₁ − 0.2x₂, in grams a minute. That is x′ = Ax with A = [−0.2 0.05; 0.2 −0.2]. A card shows it. Closed tanks shut the inlet and the drain. The pumps move 20 L/min each way. So there A = [−0.2 0.2; 0.2 −0.2]. Two masses means two equal masses between three equal springs. A fixed wall holds each end. x₁ and x₂ are how far each mass sits to the right of its rest point, in centimetres. Mass 1 feels its own spring and the middle one. So its force is −kx₁ + k(x₂ − x₁). Mass 2's force is the mirror image. So x″ = −(k/m)[2 −1; −1 2]x, with k/m = 100 per second squared. The middle spring carries a label with its stretch, x₂ − x₁, in centimetres. The state plane draws two eigenvector lines through the origin, each labelled with its eigenvalue. For open tanks they are (1, 2) with −0.1 and (1, −2) with −0.3. For closed tanks they are (1, 1) with 0 and (1, −1) with −0.4. For the masses they are (1, 1) and (−1, 1). Along (1, 1), ω² = k/m and ω = 10 rad/s. Along (−1, 1), ω² = 3k/m and ω ≈ 17.3 rad/s. Dragging the dot sets the start. For tanks it stays where each tank holds between 0 and 40 g. For masses it stays within 3 cm each way. Go starts the clock. The dot leaves a trail, and the left side moves to match. For tanks the clock runs 2 minutes each second, up to 30 minutes. For masses the motion is drawn 10 times slower than real. Each mass is let go from rest. Two faint dots ride the two lines. Each is the start's amount along its line, changing by its own rule. A acts on a mix part by part. It only stretches each eigenvector. That is why each amount can follow a rule of its own. For tanks the rule is a₀e^(λt). So each faint dot slides in towards the origin at its own rate. A faint dot whose eigenvalue is 0 stays put. For masses the rule is a₀cos(ωt). So each faint dot slides to and fro at its own speed. The real dot is always the sum of the two faint dots. It is drawn as the corner of their parallelogram. Start on a line, and the other faint dot sits at the origin. So the real dot moves straight along that line. Start anywhere else, and its trail curves. The closed tanks are the exception. There the trail runs straight, because the (1, 1) amount never changes. Readouts show x₁, x₂ and the time. Reset puts the dot back at its start. On a phone the real thing sits above the state plane. Here are the thirteen screens. Screen 1 shows the open tanks, with 30 g of salt in tank 1 and none in tank 2. Each tank's rate depends on the salt in both. So the two are linked. A card builds tank 2's rate from its flows. 20 L/min arrives from tank 1, carrying 0.2x₁ grams a minute. 20 L/min leaves, carrying 0.2x₂. So x₂′ = 0.2x₁ − 0.2x₂. Go plays it. Tank 1's salt falls. Tank 2's rises, then falls. The finished picture shows the tanks at about 5.5 minutes, both near 11.5 g. Screen 2 is a puzzle. What is tank 1's rate, x₁′? It offers −0.2x₁ + 0.05x₂, 0.2x₁ − 0.05x₂ and −0.2x₁ − 0.05x₂. The first is right. 20 L/min leaves tank 1, carrying 0.2x₁ grams a minute. 5 L/min arrives from tank 2, carrying 0.05x₂. The fresh water brings no salt. The hint says what leaves is minus and what arrives is plus. Screen 3 adds the state plane beside the tanks. One dot stands for both tanks at once, at (x₁, x₂). It is also called the phase plane. It draws the two eigenvector lines, (1, 2) with −0.1 and (1, −2) with −0.3. They add to the trace, −0.4. They multiply to the determinant, 0.03. From (30, 0), Go draws a curved trail in to the origin. The finished picture shows the whole trail. Screen 4 is a puzzle. The dot starts at (10, 20), on the (1, 2) line. Where does it go? It offers straight along the line to the origin, curving off the line, and round onto the (1, −2) line. The first is right. A(10, 20) = (−1, −2). That is −0.1 times (10, 20). So the rate points straight back along the line. The dot never leaves it. It shrinks as 10e^(−0.1t) lots of (1, 2). Go checks it. The hint says to work out A times (10, 20) and compare it with (10, 20). Screen 5 shows the faint dots, back at the start (30, 0). That start is 15 lots of (1, 2) plus 15 lots of (1, −2). Check it: 15(1, 2) + 15(1, −2) = (30, 0). Call the amounts a and b. A only stretches each eigenvector. So A turns a(1, 2) + b(1, −2) into −0.1a(1, 2) − 0.3b(1, −2). Each amount gets its own rate, a′ = −0.1a and b′ = −0.3b. So the equations are called decoupled. So a = 15e^(−0.1t) and b = 15e^(−0.3t). Go plays it. The faint dots slide in along their lines. The real dot is their sum. The finished picture shows all three dots at 5 minutes. Screen 6 is a puzzle. From (30, 0), how much of b is left after 10 minutes? It offers about 0.75, about 5.5 and 0. About 0.75 is right. 15e^(−0.3 × 10) = 15e^(−3) ≈ 0.75. About 5.5 is 15e^(−1). It uses the (1, 2) line's rate. 0 is wrong, because a decay never quite reaches zero. The hint says each amount uses its own line's eigenvalue. Screen 7 adds the parts back. x₁ = 15e^(−0.1t) + 15e^(−0.3t) and x₂ = 30e^(−0.1t) − 30e^(−0.3t) grams. Tank 2 is fullest after about 5.5 minutes, at about 11.5 g. At that moment the two tanks match. The fast part dies first. So the trail bends onto the (1, 2) line. When you applied a matrix step after step, the eigenvalue biggest in size took over. With e^(λt), the larger eigenvalue takes over instead. Here that is −0.1, the one nearer zero. The view zooms in as the dot shrinks, keeping tank 2's fullest moment in sight. The finished picture shows the trail at 30 minutes, bending onto the (1, 2) line. Screen 8 is a puzzle. At 30 minutes the dot is nearly on which line? It offers the (1, 2) line, the (1, −2) line and the x₁ axis. The first is right. The slow amount is 15e^(−3) ≈ 0.75. The fast one is 15e^(−9), under 0.01. So tank 2 holds about twice tank 1, about 1.49 g to 0.75 g. The hint asks which amount dies faster. Screen 9 switches to the two masses. A card shows x″ = −(k/m)[2 −1; −1 2]x. That is the matrix B whose eigenvectors you found. Its eigenvalue is 1 along (1, 1) and 3 along (−1, 1). Each mode swings with ω² = (k/m)λ. From (2, 2) cm, Go swings both masses together. The dot slides to and fro along the (1, 1) line. The middle spring's stretch reads 0 the whole time. So only the outer springs pull. Then ω² = k/m = 100, so ω = 10 rad/s. A swing like this is called a normal mode. Then from (−2, 2) cm they swing opposite ways along the (−1, 1) line. The middle spring stretches and squashes by up to 4 cm, twice each mass's shift. So each mass feels k from its outer spring and 2k from the middle one. That makes ω² = 3k/m. The finished picture shows both trails on their lines. Screen 10 is a puzzle. With k/m = 100 per second squared, how fast does the opposite mode swing? It offers about 17.3 rad/s, 300 rad/s and 30 rad/s. About 17.3 rad/s is right. Along (−1, 1), the eigenvalue of (k/m)B is 3k/m = 300. That is ω², so ω = √300 ≈ 17.3. 300 rad/s takes ω as the eigenvalue itself. 30 rad/s is 3 × 10. The hint says the eigenvalue is ω², not ω. Screen 11 shows a start off both lines. Mass 2 is pulled 2 cm and let go, at (0, 2). That is 1 lot of (1, 1) plus 1 lot of (−1, 1). The faint dots swing along their lines, one at 10 rad/s and one at about 17.3 rad/s. The real dot is their sum. So its trail weaves to and fro across a diamond-shaped box. The middle spring now stretches and squashes. So the masses' shudder is just the two simple swings added. The two lines also happen to be at right angles, since (1, 1) · (−1, 1) = 0. Each eigenvalue sets its swing's speed. The finished picture shows the trail after 2 seconds of real time. Screen 12 is a mixed puzzle. The masses start at (3, 1) cm. How much of each mode is that? It offers 2 of (1, 1) and −1 of (−1, 1), 3 of (1, 1) and 1 of (−1, 1), and 2 of (1, 1) and 1 of (−1, 1). The first is right, since 2(1, 1) − 1(−1, 1) = (3, 1). 3 and 1 just copies the start's numbers. 2 and 1 gives (1, 3). The hint says to solve a − b = 3 and a + b = 1. Go then shows the faint dots starting at (2, 2) and (1, −1). Screen 13 is a mixed puzzle on the closed tanks. Tank 1 starts with 30 g. Where does the dot head? It offers (15, 15), (0, 0) and (30, 0). (15, 15) is right. The start is 15 lots of (1, 1) plus 15 lots of (1, −1). The (1, 1) amount has eigenvalue 0. Since e^(0t) = 1, it stays at 15. The (1, −1) amount dies as e^(−0.4t). No salt can leave, so the total stays 30 g. The hint asks what e^(0t) equals. Go checks it. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. The finish panel says where you meet this. A propulsion shaft's discs act as the masses and its lengths of shaft as the springs. Its natural frequencies are the square roots of the eigenvalues, and a drive near one makes it resonate. Linked circuits and a two-equation dive model come apart the same way. Complex eigenvalues make the parts ring as they fade.
interactive.ignores: In the open tanks, each tank's salt is drawn shrinking towards nothing. It never quite gets there. Each fading part only falls by the same fraction each minute. The tank clock is sped up to 2 minutes a second. The masses are slowed 10 times. Each tank is taken as perfectly mixed, so every drop leaving it has the tank's strength. Real tanks take time to mix. The springs are ideal and nothing rubs, so the masses swing for ever. Real swings die away as friction takes their energy. The plane shows the masses' positions only, so each start is let go from rest. A start with a push needs their two speeds as well. The eigenvector lines run on past the edge of the plane. The tank figures and k/m are example values.

explain.text:
Two tanks joined by pipes change together. The salt in each tank changes at a rate that depends on the salt in both. So the rates are a matrix times the amounts, x′ = Ax. Measure the amounts along A's eigenvectors, and the link comes apart. Each part then changes on its own. Its own eigenvalue sets its rate. The real motion is just those parts added back together.

Take two 100 L tanks of brine. Fresh water runs into tank 1 at 15 L/min. A pump sends 20 L/min from tank 1 to tank 2. Another 5 L/min runs back. The other 15 L/min drains out of tank 2. Each flow carries salt at its tank's strength. That strength is the tank's grams divided by 100 L. What leaves a tank is minus and what arrives is plus. So x₁′ = −0.2x₁ + 0.05x₂ and x₂′ = 0.2x₁ − 0.2x₂, in grams a minute. That is x′ = Ax with A = [−0.2 0.05; 0.2 −0.2]. You solve linked tanks like these with the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A.[^1] Here the eigenvalues are −0.1 along (1, 2) and −0.3 along (1, −2). They add to the trace, −0.4. They multiply to the determinant, 0.03.

Now write the salt as a lots of (1, 2) plus b lots of (1, −2). A acts on a mix part by part. It only stretches each eigenvector. So a′ = −0.1a and b′ = −0.3b. Each amount changes by its own rule and ignores the other. Equations like these are [[decoupled]]. Each one is the plain decay rule from differential equations. So a = a₀e^(−0.1t) and b = b₀e^(−0.3t). Start with 30 g in tank 1 and none in tank 2. That is 15 lots of each. Check it: 15(1, 2) + 15(1, −2) = (30, 0). Add the parts back to get x₂ = 30e^(−0.1t) − 30e^(−0.3t) grams. Tank 2 fills to about 11.5 g after about 5.5 minutes, when the tanks match. Then it drains. Plot both tanks as one dot (x₁, x₂) and you have the [[state plane]]. It is also called the phase plane. Start the dot on an eigenvector line and it runs straight along it. The other amount starts at zero. Zero times e^(λt) stays zero. Start it anywhere else, and the fast part dies first. So its path bends onto the slow line. When you applied a matrix step after step, the eigenvalue biggest in size took over. With e^(λt), the larger eigenvalue takes over instead, as long as the start has some of it. Here that is −0.1.

Two equal masses on three equal springs work the same way. Mass 1 feels its own spring and the middle one. So its force is −kx₁ + k(x₂ − x₁). Mass 2's force is the mirror image. So x″ = −(k/m)Bx. Here B = [2 −1; −1 2], the matrix whose eigenvectors you have already found. Along an eigenvector, B only stretches, by its eigenvalue λ. So each amount obeys a″ = −(k/m)λa. That is the spring rule from differential equations. Along (1, 1) the masses move together, with ω² = k/m. Along (−1, 1) they move opposite ways, with ω² = 3k/m.[^2] In the together swing, the middle spring keeps its length. So only the outer springs pull. In the opposite swing, the middle spring stretches by twice each mass's shift. So each mass feels k from its outer spring and 2k from the middle one, 3k in all. These simple swings are the [[normal mode]]s. Any motion of the pair is a sum of them.[^3] With k/m = 100 per second squared, they swing at 10 and about 17.3 radians a second. The second is √300, not 300. That is because 3k/m = 300 is ω², not ω. Both systems are teaching models. Real tanks never mix perfectly. Real springs lose energy, so real swings die away. So the masses' shudder hides two simple swings, one together and one opposite. Each one's eigenvalue sets its speed. **When A has a full set of eigenvectors, linked change comes apart along them. The system moves as a sum of simple modes, each at the rate its own eigenvalue sets.**

analogy.text: Picture two equal rooms side by side, sharing one wall, with the heating off. Measure each room's temperature as how far it sits above the outdoor one. Each room loses heat outside through its own walls. Heat also crosses the shared wall from the warmer room to the cooler. Any start splits into an average part and a difference part. The average falls only through the outside walls, so it fades slowly. The difference also leaks across the shared wall, so it fades faster. Each part fades on its own clock. The two rooms' temperatures are their sum.
analogy.breaks: A real room is not one temperature. Its air sits in layers, and its walls store heat. The weather outside changes too. Rooms of different sizes tilt the two directions away from a plain average and difference. The tanks' unequal flows do the same, giving (1, 2) and (1, −2).

practice.text:
- Name the amounts, x₁ and x₂. They might be the salt in each tank or each mass's position.
- Write each rate from the flows or forces. For a tank, each flow carries salt at its tank's strength, which is salt ÷ volume. What leaves is minus and what arrives is plus.
- Collect the numbers into A, so x′ = Ax. For masses on springs, write x″ = −Kx. The springs give you K.
- Find the eigenvalues from λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0. Then find an eigenvector for each. Check the eigenvalues add to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
- Split the start into amounts of each eigenvector. Solve a × (first eigenvector) + b × (second) = start.
- Give each amount its own motion. For x′ = Ax it is a₀e^(λt). For x″ = −Kx with a start from rest, it is a₀cos(ωt), with ω = √λ.
- Add the parts back. Put t = 0 in to check you get the start.

**Rules of thumb:** for x′ = Ax, a negative eigenvalue gives a part that dies away. The more negative it is, the faster. An eigenvalue of 0 gives a steady state, a part that never changes. A positive one gives a part that grows. Complex eigenvalues give a part that rings, like the underdamped spring.[^4] With real eigenvalues, the larger one's part takes over in the end, as long as the start has some of it. For springs each eigenvalue is ω², so take its square root.

**Worked example:** the two tanks, A = [−0.2 0.05; 0.2 −0.2] per minute. The eigenvalues are −0.1 with (1, 2) and −0.3 with (1, −2). Start with 30 g in tank 1 and none in tank 2. Solve a + b = 30 and 2a − 2b = 0. That gives a = b = 15. Then x₂ = 30e^(−0.1t) − 30e^(−0.3t). It is largest when its rate is zero. That happens when 3e^(−0.1t) = 9e^(−0.3t). So e^(0.2t) = 3, and t = 5 ln 3 ≈ 5.49 minutes. Then tank 2 holds about 11.5 g, the same as tank 1. After 30 minutes the fast part is under 0.01 g. Tank 1 holds about 0.75 g and tank 2 about 1.49 g. That is close to the 1 : 2 of the slow line.

**Where you meet it:** any linked system whose rates are fixed multiples of its amounts. Mixing tanks, heat passing between rooms and masses on springs can all be written this way. A propulsion shaft's twisting is worked out the same way. Discs along the shaft play the masses. The lengths of shaft between them play the springs. Its natural frequencies are the square roots of the eigenvalues. Drive the shaft near one of them, and it resonates.[^5] Two linked circuits, or a submarine's two-equation dive model, are solved the same way. You can also write the whole answer at once as a matrix exponential, e^(At). Splitting along the eigenvectors gives the same answer with tools you already have.

**Common mistakes**
- A sign slip in A. What leaves a tank is minus. What arrives is plus.
- Giving a part the other line's rate. Each e^(λt) goes with its own eigenvector.
- Taking ω as the eigenvalue itself. For springs the eigenvalue is ω², so ω is its square root.
- Reading the start's numbers as mode amounts. (3, 1) cm is 2 lots of (1, 1) and −1 lot of (−1, 1), not 3 and 1.
- Expecting the tanks to empty. Each part only shrinks by the same fraction each minute. It never reaches zero.
- Expecting a mixed start to repeat neatly. The two swings' rates are not in a whole-number ratio here. So the pattern never quite repeats.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the real dot staying the sum of two faint dots when you drag the start dot and press Go. Each faint dot rides its own eigenvector line at its own rate.

checks.label: Linked tanks lead to a linear system of differential equations, solved with the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of its matrix: for the open and the closed tanks, the eigenvector parts added up obey the rates x′ = Ax at every moment, from every corner of the drag square and from the lesson’s starts
(1, 1) is an eigenvector of the masses’ matrix with eigenvalue k/m, and (−1, 1) one with eigenvalue 3k/m

The most general motion of the masses is a sum of the simple swings, the normal modes: from starts all over the drag square, each faint dot alone obeys x″ = −(k/m)Bx, and the dot drawn is always their sum

Every worked number is right: A = [−0.2 0.05; 0.2 −0.2] from the flows, with the drain at 15 L/min; trace −0.4, determinant 0.03, eigenvalues −0.1 and −0.3; (30, 0) = 15(1, 2) + 15(1, −2); tank 2 fullest at 5 ln 3 ≈ 5.5 min with about 11.5 g, level with tank 1; b ≈ 0.75 after 10 minutes and 15e^(−1) ≈ 5.5; (0.75, 1.49) at 30 minutes with the fast part under 0.01; A(10, 20) = (−1, −2); the closed tanks’ 0 and −0.4, heading for (15, 15) with 30 g in all; B = [2 −1; −1 2], ω = 10 and about 17.3 rad/s; (0, 2) and (3, 1) split as (1, 1) and (2, −1); the together swing never stretches the middle spring and the opposite one stretches it by up to 4 cm
Each puzzle’s answer comes from the rule, and each wrong answer offered is the slip its hint names
Each puzzle offers three different answers, accepts only the right one, and draws every wrong one in the warning colour
Before Check, no puzzle shows its answer; after a right answer, it does

Each demonstration ends where the lesson says: the tanks level at about 11.5 g after about 5.5 minutes; a curved trail from (30, 0) in to the origin; the parts 15e^(−0.5)(1, 2) and 15e^(−1.5)(1, −2) at 5 minutes, adding to the dot; at 30 minutes the dot on the (1, 2) line, with tank 2’s fullest moment marked; one trail on each mode’s line, the second start stretching the middle spring by 4 cm; after 2 s from (0, 2), a trail that weaves inside its box

While each demonstration plays, the rule holds at every moment: the dot is where the rule puts it, each part is on its own line and changes only by its own e^(λt) or cos(ωt), the parts add up to the dot, and no tank holds less than nothing or more than 40 g
Dragging the start: near an eigenvector line it lands exactly on it, so the other part sits at the origin and the dot runs straight along the line; anywhere else it stays inside the drag square
After a right answer on the 30-minute puzzle, the view zooms in by itself so the dot and both parts stay in sight as they shrink, and the key names the grid spacing drawn
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer’s motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

steps: How fast is the opposite swing?

applied.problem: Says every tank faint dot slides in to the origin and every off-line start curves, but in the closed tanks the (1, 1) amount has eigenvalue 0, so its dot stays put and the trail runs straight, e.g. (30, 0) straight to (15, 15).
Says each tank's salt is drawn shrinking towards nothing, but in the closed tanks the salt settles at 15 g each, and the (1, 1) part never falls at all.
Different rates alone do not stop a pattern repeating: swings in a whole-number ratio repeat exactly. Here 17.3 : 10 is √3, not such a ratio, so the claim needs narrowing.
